question.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ),$ given by

$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨5\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

parametrizes one sheet of the hyperboloid of two sheets defined in Cartesian coordinates as 

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-{z}^{2}=-1.
$$

 

By first considering the transformations

$$
x=5X,\,y=2Y,\,z=Z
$$

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the third component of $f.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola ${Z}^{2}-{r}^{2}={k}^{2}$ can be parametrized as $⟨Z,r⟩=⟨k\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,k\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩$* for $ϕ\in R.$

current_example.problem:
The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi),$ given by 

$$
\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) =  \big\langle \text{_____}, \: 3\sinh{\phi} \sin\theta, \: 3\cosh{\phi} \big\rangle
$$

parametrizes one sheet of the hyperboloid of two sheets defined in Cartesian coordinates as $x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = -9.$ By expressing the equation of the hyperboloid in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the first component of $\mathbf{f}.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola $z^2-r^2 = k^2$ can be parametrized as $\langle z,r\rangle = \langle k\cosh\phi, k\sinh \phi\rangle$* for $\phi\in \mathbb R.$
current_example.worked_solution:
If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad

y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 

z = z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-9 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-9 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-{z}^{2} & =-9 \\ {r}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-9 \\ {z}^{2}-{r}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the hyperbola $z^2 - r^2 = 9$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14284340/assets/4e7b508432f12b8dc98e37ae2786d220eb97bdc58fe5a29c5f7728cac46471f0.png)

Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

$$
\langle z, r \rangle = \langle 3\cosh{\phi}, \: 3\sinh{\phi} \rangle,
\qquad \phi \in \mathbb R.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩ \\  & =⟨(3\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,(3\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$ and $\phi \in \mathbb R.$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}3\sinh{\phi} \cos\theta} .$
